entries.sentence: The NHS offers babies and children vaccines against many serious illnesses, from 8 weeks old through school, and a GP surgery can arrange any that are missed.
entries.note: NHS page lists routine vaccines by age from 8 weeks; GP surgery can book or rearrange; catch-up possible for most.

entries.sentence: The NHS lists routine childhood vaccines by age, starting with the babies' visits at 8, 12 and 16 weeks.
entries.note: Search result for the NHS page: lists routine vaccines by age, starting with babies' doses at 8, 12 and 16 weeks.

entries.sentence: From 1 January 2026 the MMRV vaccine, which adds chickenpox protection, replaced MMR in the routine schedule for children.
entries.note: Local NHS and NHS inform pages: MMRV (measles, mumps, rubella, chickenpox) added to routine schedule on 1 January 2026, replaces MMR. Not read on the nhs.uk page itself.

entries.sentence: Older children are offered HPV in Year 8, and MenACWY and the 3-in-1 teenage booster in Year 9, according to UKHSA and NHS pages.
entries.note: UKHSA adolescent briefing and NHS trust pages: HPV Year 8; MenACWY and Td/IPV Year 9; some areas differ.

entries.sentence: The NHS says it is best to have vaccines on time, but most can still be caught up if missed, and a GP surgery can arrange this.
entries.note: NHS page: best on time, can still catch up on most; GP surgery can book or rearrange.

entries.sentence: Redness or swelling where the needle went in and a fever are common after vaccines, and a young baby with a high temperature is a reason to contact the GP urgently.
entries.note: GOV.UK baby guide: redness, swelling, tenderness, fever common. NHS inform Scotland: contact GP urgently if young baby (under 3 months) has high temperature or fever lasts 48 hours.

entries.sentence: The NHS lists the routine vaccines by age, and its table starts with the babies' visits at 8, 12 and 16 weeks.
entries.note: NHS page lists routine vaccines by age starting with babies' doses at 8, 12 and 16 weeks.

entries.sentence: The 6-in-1 vaccine helps protect against six serious illnesses: diphtheria, hepatitis B, Hib, polio, tetanus and whooping cough.
entries.note: NHS 6-in-1 page lists the six diseases.

entries.sentence: The GOV.UK schedule for 1 July 2026 places rotavirus and MenB vaccines at the early visits, and the pneumococcal vaccine at 16 weeks.
entries.note: Search summary of the GOV.UK schedule: 6-in-1 at 8, 12, 16 weeks, rotavirus and MenB at early visits, PCV at 16 weeks.

entries.sentence: Rotavirus vaccine is for a stomach bug, MenB is for a type of meningitis bacteria, and the pneumococcal vaccine is named for the pneumococcus germ.
entries.note: Plain-language gloss of the vaccine names; not stated in the returned text.

entries.sentence: The GOV.UK schedule lists the pneumococcal and MenB vaccines again at one year.
entries.note: Search summary: the same page places PCV, MenB and MMRV at one year.

entries.sentence: The NHS page also covers extra vaccines for children in at-risk groups, such as those with long-term conditions or a weakened immune system.
entries.note: Search summary of NHS page: extra vaccines offered to at-risk groups, e.g. chronic conditions or weakened immune system.

entries.sentence: According to the NHS, children born on or after 1 July 2024 are offered a fourth dose of the 6-in-1 vaccine at 18 months.
entries.note: Search results: 4th 6-in-1 at 18 months for children born on or after 1 July 2024; NHS 6-in-1 page lists 18 months.

entries.sentence: For those children the Hib/MenC vaccine was dropped, and the GOV.UK schedule no longer lists it.
entries.note: GOV.UK update note: schedule no longer includes the discontinued Hib/MenC Menitorix; search result: dropped for children born on or after 1 July 2024.

entries.sentence: The NHS table also lists a pre-school booster against diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough and polio at 3 years and 4 months.
entries.note: Search results: NHS table shows 4-in-1 pre-school booster at 3 years 4 months; GOV.UK lists dTaP/IPV pre-school booster at around 3 years 4 months.

entries.sentence: Children born before 1 July 2024 follow an earlier version of the schedule, so GOV.UK publishes a separate table for them.
entries.note: Search results: some pages say children born before 1 July 2024 follow a different pattern; a separate GOV.UK schedule for children born on or before 30 June 2024 exists.

entries.sentence: The MMRV vaccine protects against measles, mumps, rubella and chickenpox, and it was added to the routine schedule on 1 January 2026.
entries.note: Local NHS pages and NHS inform describe MMRV added from 1 January 2026.

entries.sentence: NHS pages describe two doses, at 12 months and at 18 months, which brings the second measles, mumps and rubella dose forward from 3 years and 4 months.
entries.note: Lincolnshire ICB: second dose of MMR part brought forward from 3y4m to 18 months; NHS inform: 12 and 18 months (Scotland timetable; England wording from search summary).

entries.sentence: A catch-up offer of chickenpox vaccine for some older children is described on GOV.UK, but sources give different start dates.
entries.note: GOV.UK says 1 November 2026 to 31 March 2028 for children born between 1 January 2020 and 31 August 2022; another source says 26 November 2026.

entries.sentence: Scotland runs its own programme, and NHS inform gives a different timetable from England's.
entries.note: Search summary: NHS inform Scotland describes a different timetable.

entries.sentence: School teams offer HPV vaccine to boys and girls in Year 8, to protect against genital warts and cancers linked to HPV.
entries.note: Search summary of UKHSA adolescent programme and NHS pages.

entries.sentence: The MenACWY vaccine and the 3-in-1 teenage booster, called Td/IPV, are offered in Year 9, although some areas say Year 9 or 10.
entries.note: Search summary: MenACWY and Td/IPV offered in Year 9; some regional sites say Year 9 or 10.

entries.sentence: The NHS says the children's flu vaccine is offered to 2 and 3 year olds, to pupils from reception to Year 11, and to children with certain long-term conditions.
entries.note: NHS child flu page via search summary.

entries.sentence: Most school-age children have it at school in the autumn term, and the usual form is a nasal spray.
entries.note: NHS child flu page: most get it at school, autumn term; nasal spray.

entries.sentence: Children turning 18 move on to the adult injected flu vaccine, and some pharmacies may offer the vaccine to eligible children, with the NHS page setting out which.
entries.note: Search summary: children turning 18 move to adult injected vaccine; participating pharmacies; check NHS page for rules.

entries.sentence: An injected version is offered if the spray is unsuitable, including for families who do not accept the pork gelatine in the spray.
entries.note: NHS child flu page: injection for those who cannot have the spray; pork gelatine.

entries.sentence: Common flu spray side effects listed by the NHS include a blocked or runny nose, loss of appetite, tiredness and headache.
entries.note: NHS child flu page side effects.

entries.sentence: The NHS says a GP surgery can book or rearrange a vaccination appointment.
entries.note: NHS page: GP surgery can book or rearrange an appointment.

entries.sentence: The NHS says it is best to have vaccines on time, but most can still be caught up if they are missed.
entries.note: NHS page: best to have on time, can still catch up on most.

entries.sentence: For the 6-in-1 vaccine, the NHS says a child can still have it up to the age of 10.
entries.note: NHS 6-in-1 page via search summary.

entries.sentence: Children who miss school sessions can catch up at a community clinic or at the GP, and those who are home educated can be offered flu vaccine at a community clinic.
entries.note: Search summaries: missed pupils catch up via community clinics or GP; home-educated children offered flu at a community clinic; from 14 GP practice for HPV, MenACWY, 3-in-1.

entries.sentence: Young people starting university are advised to check their MenACWY, MMR and HPV vaccines, and the NHS says a GP can still give MenACWY until the 25th birthday.
entries.note: Search summary of NHS page.

entries.sentence: For anything unclear about a child's own schedule, the NHS and GOV.UK pages that match the child's birth date apply.
entries.note: Search summaries advise checking the page matching the child's birth date.

entries.sentence: The GOV.UK guide for babies says redness, swelling or tenderness where the injection was given is common, and it goes away without treatment.
entries.note: Search summary: little redness, swelling or tenderness at injection site that disappears on its own; irritability and fever common.

entries.sentence: For the 6-in-1 vaccine, the NHS lists swelling or pain where the injection was given, a high temperature, tiredness and loss of appetite.
entries.note: Search summary of NHS 6-in-1 page: injection-site swelling or pain, high temperature, tiredness, loss of appetite.

entries.sentence: Irritability and fever are also common, and fever is more likely when the MenB vaccine is given with other vaccines.
entries.note: Search summary: fever more common with MenB alongside other vaccines.

entries.sentence: Allergic reactions are very rare and usually start within minutes, and the people giving vaccines are trained to treat them straight away.
entries.note: Search summary: very rare, within minutes, staff trained to treat immediately.

entries.sentence: For a serious one, called anaphylaxis, the sources say it happens about once in every million immunisations.
entries.note: Search summary: anaphylaxis about once in every million immunisations.

entries.sentence: NHS inform Scotland advises contacting the GP urgently if a baby under 3 months has a high temperature, or if a fever lasts 48 hours after vaccination.
entries.note: Search summary: contact GP urgently if under 3 months with high temperature or fever continues 48 hours.

entries.sentence: The NHS says a flu vaccination may be postponed if a child is unwell on the day.
entries.note: Search summary caveat: may be postponed if child unwell, e.g. high temperature.
